\chapter{Such, Which, Then, But Rather}
\label{ch:tal-y-salvo}
\hlchaptermodality{329}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can join and correct two thoughts with tal, cual, pues, sino and salvo, and say why sino needs a no earlier in the sentence.}

Complete ES-C329-salvo: pair tal with cual, conclude with pues, correct a negative with sino, and make an exception with salvo.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tal]{tal — the \emph{such} you have been saying inside \emph{tal vez}}

\label{lesson:ES-C329-tal}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{almost}, then \emph{even}. (\emph{Casi}; \emph{incluso}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item tal vez — the hedge you already use. This is its first word.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{TAL}, one beat, and the \emph{l} is made with the tongue tip forward and the back of the tongue flat — never the dark, swallowed \emph{l} that ends English \emph{tall}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{tal} — \textquotedblleft{}such,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}such a,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}of that kind.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{tālis} meant \emph{of that kind}. It is the answering half of a pair: \emph{qualis} asked \emph{of what kind?} and \emph{talis} replied \emph{of that kind}. You will meet its partner in the very next lesson.

You have been saying it for a long time without opening it. \textbf{Tal vez} is \emph{tal} plus \emph{vez} — \emph{such a turn}, \emph{a turn of that kind} — which is how Spanish says \emph{maybe}. Every time you hedged with \emph{tal vez} you were saying \emph{in a case like that}.

English lost the word as a word, but kept it in two places worth knowing.

To \textbf{retaliate} is \textbf{re-} plus \textbf{tālis}: \emph{to give back the like}. Not merely to strike back, but to return something \emph{of that same kind} — the word carries its own measure of proportion.

And lawyers still say \textbf{lex talionis}, the \emph{law of the like}, which is the formal name for the rule that an eye should answer an eye. That is \emph{tālis} doing the work it was born for: matching a thing to its kind.

Spanish also uses \emph{tal} in a question you will hear constantly — \textbf{¿qué tal?}, roughly \emph{what kind of?}, which has settled into meaning \emph{how's it going?}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five small joining words. These are the pieces that let two thoughts lean on each other.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tal}
  \item \emph{tal vez}
  \item \emph{tal vez no}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{tālis} mean? (Of that kind.) And what does \textbf{retaliate} mean piece by piece? (To give back the like.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cual]{cual — the question \emph{tal} was answering}

\label{lesson:ES-C329-cual}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{even}, then \emph{such}. (\emph{Incluso}; \emph{tal}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item lo cual — the connector this word already lives in.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{KWAL}, one beat. The \emph{cu-} is a \emph{k} followed straight by a \emph{w} glide, and the \emph{a} stays open. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{cual} — \textquotedblleft{}which,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}as,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}of what kind.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{quālis} asked the question that \textbf{tālis} answered. \emph{Quālis?} — \emph{of what kind?} \emph{Tālis.} — \emph{of that kind.} The two words were built to be used together, and Spanish still pairs them: \textbf{tal cual} means \emph{exactly as it is}, literally \emph{such as which}.

You already carry it in \textbf{lo cual}, the connector for referring back to a whole clause.

Now the English payoff, and it is a good one. Cicero needed a Latin word for a Greek philosophical idea — the \emph{what-kind-ness} of a thing, as opposed to its \emph{how-much-ness}. He built one out of \emph{quālis}: \textbf{quālitās}. That word came into English as \textbf{quality}.

So \emph{quality} does not originally mean \emph{goodness} at all. It means \emph{the kind of thing something is}. That older sense is still visible when a chemist speaks of \textbf{qualitative} analysis, which asks \emph{what is in it?} rather than \emph{how much?} — and its partner \textbf{quantitative} is built the same way on \emph{quantus}, \emph{how much}.

A \textbf{qualification} is likewise a statement of what kind, which is why qualifying a claim narrows what kind of claim it is.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of five. \emph{Tal} and \emph{cual} are a matched pair, and Spanish uses them as one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cual}
  \item \emph{lo cual}
  \item \emph{tal cual}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{quālis} ask? (Of what kind?) And which everyday English noun did Cicero build on it? (\emph{Quality}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pues]{pues — the word already hiding in \emph{después}}

\label{lesson:ES-C329-pues}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{such}, then \emph{which}. (\emph{Tal}; \emph{cual}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item después — this word is inside it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PWES}, one beat. The \emph{ue} is a single glide, \emph{w} into \emph{e}, not two separate vowels. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{pues} — \textquotedblleft{}well,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}then,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}since.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{post} meant \emph{after}. Spanish softened it into \textbf{pues}, and in doing so let it drift from time into reasoning: \emph{after that} became \emph{therefore}, and \emph{therefore} became the small \emph{well...} that a speaker puts at the front of a sentence while deciding what to say.

That drift is ordinary. English \emph{then} does the same double duty — \emph{I ate, then I left} is time, but \emph{if that is so, then you are wrong} is logic.

You already own the compound. \textbf{Después} is three Latin words stacked up: \textbf{de ex post}, \emph{from out of after}. Speakers kept adding reinforcement to \emph{post} until it was three syllables long, and \emph{pues} is the bare original that survived alongside it.

English never softened the word at all. It uses \textbf{post} raw and everywhere: a \textbf{post-war} year, a \textbf{postscript} written after, to \textbf{postpone} is to place after, \textbf{posterior} is the back, and a \textbf{post mortem} happens after death.

In speech, \emph{pues} is one of the most common words in the language, and often carries almost no meaning — it is the sound of somebody taking a breath before answering.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three of five. You have \emph{of that kind}, \emph{of what kind}, and now \emph{therefore}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pues}
  \item \emph{pues sí}
  \item \emph{pues no, gracias}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{post} mean? (After.) And which three Latin words are stacked inside \emph{después}? (\emph{De ex post}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sino]{sino — two words fused into one, and both of them are yours}

\label{lesson:ES-C329-sino}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{which}, then \emph{well, then}. (\emph{Cual}; \emph{pues}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item no ... nada — the double negative this word belongs with.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SI-no}, two even beats, the weight on the first. Both vowels are short and pure. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sino} — \textquotedblleft{}but rather.\textquotedblright{}

This one is built from two words you already have, welded together: \textbf{si} (\emph{if}, Latin \textbf{sī}) plus \textbf{no} (Latin \textbf{nōn}). \emph{Si no} — \emph{if not}.

Spanish uses it for a specific job that English handles clumsily. \emph{Sino} does not merely oppose; it \textbf{corrects a negative}. First you deny something, then \emph{sino} supplies the right answer in its place.

Watch the shape. \emph{No hoy, sino mañana} — \emph{not today, but rather tomorrow}. The \emph{no} opens a hole and the \emph{sino} fills it. English has to lean on \emph{but rather} or \emph{but instead}, because plain \emph{but} is doing a different job.

That is why Spanish keeps two words where English has one. \textbf{Pero} contrasts two things that are both true. \textbf{Sino} replaces something that was denied. Listen for the \emph{no} that comes before it: with one in the sentence, \emph{sino} fits; with none, \emph{pero} is the word you want.

Written as one word it is the conjunction. Written as two — \emph{si no} — it is still the plain \emph{if not} it was born as, and Spanish speakers have to keep the spelling straight for exactly that reason.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four of five. This is the first of these joiners that changes the shape of a whole sentence rather than colouring one word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sino}
  \item \emph{no hoy, sino mañana}
  \item \emph{no aquí, sino así}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two words are fused into \emph{sino}? (\emph{Si} and \emph{no} — if not.) And what has to appear earlier in the sentence for \emph{sino} to be right? (A \emph{no}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[salvo]{salvo — the second half of \emph{sano y salvo}}

\label{lesson:ES-C329-salvo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{well, then}, then \emph{but rather}. (\emph{Pues}; \emph{sino}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item sano — the word this one is normally said next to.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SAL-vo}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{v} is soft, made without the lips quite closing, so it lands between an English \emph{v} and \emph{b}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{salvo} — \textquotedblleft{}except,\textquotedblright{} and, as an adjective, \textquotedblleft{}safe.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{salvus} meant \emph{unharmed, whole, in one piece}. Spanish kept it in both of those jobs, and you have already met one of them.

In the last chapter, \emph{sano} came with the set phrase \textbf{sano y salvo} — \emph{healthy and unharmed}, which English says as \emph{safe and sound} with the two halves in the other order. That \emph{salvo} is this word, and now it stands on its own.

The second job is the surprising one. If everything in a group is unharmed \textbf{except} one thing, then that one thing has been set aside — and \emph{salvo} slid from \emph{safe} into \emph{excepted}. \textbf{Todo salvo eso} is \emph{everything except that}. The excepted item is the one left standing outside the harm.

English inherited the root generously. To \textbf{salvage} is to bring something out unharmed. \textbf{Salvation} is being made whole. A \textbf{salve} heals. A \textbf{salver} was a tasting-tray that kept a nobleman safe from poison. A naval \textbf{salvo} was a salute — a wish for safety, fired from guns.

And English \textbf{safe} is the same word, arriving by a different road through French \emph{sauf}, which is why \emph{sauf} still means \emph{except} in French to this day.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five joiners: \emph{tal}, \emph{cual}, \emph{pues}, \emph{sino}, \emph{salvo}. With these you can qualify, correct, conclude and make an exception — the machinery of an argument, in five short words.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{salvo}
  \item \emph{sano y salvo}
  \item \emph{todo salvo hoy}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{salvus} mean? (Unharmed, whole.) And how does \emph{salvo} get from \emph{safe} to \emph{except}? (The excepted thing is the one left unharmed.)
\end{tcolorbox}
